sentences.text: Gregory S. Paul estimated this dinosaur to be two meters long and to weigh 175 kilograms in 2010.
It possessed a skull featuring a pair of long brow horns that resemble those found in Ceratopsidae.
In 2009, Sues and Averianov found that the animal possessed both basal traits indicating a lower evolutionary position and derived traits indicating a higher position.
This species provides important evidence that double-rooted maxillae and predentary teeth appeared earlier in Asian ceratopsians than in North American ones.
The species Turanoceratops tardabilis was validly named in 1989 by Nesov, Kaznysjkina, and Cherepanov.
The generic name combines Turan, an old Persian name for Turkestan, and ceratops, meaning horned face.
The specific name tardabilis means retarding in Latin, referring to the long duration of the research.
Authentic material also includes postorbitals with brow horn cores, teeth, a predentary, and limb elements.
Turanoceratops was a herbivore, feeding on plants like ferns and conifers.
Turanoceratops belongs to Ceratopsia, a group of herbivorous dinosaurs with a parrot-like beak that lived in Asia and North America during the Cretaceous period until the end of the dinosaur era.
The animal is classified in the class Ornithischia.
The parent group of Turanoceratops is Ceratopsoidea.
Turanoceratops is classified within the family Ceratopsidae.
A 2009 study by Hans-Dieter Sues concluded that Turanoceratops was a true member of the family Ceratopsidae.
A 2009 study led by Hans-Dieter Sues concluded that Turanoceratops represents a true member of the family Ceratopsidae.
Turanoceratops lived roughly 90 million years ago during the mid-late Turonian stage of the late Cretaceous period.
Turanoceratops lived from 93.9 to 89.8 million years ago during the Turonian stage.
Some scientists, including Andrew Farke, disagree with the classification of Turanoceratops as a true Ceratopsid, arguing instead that it is a close relative but not a member of the clade.
